title: Question 1.2
statement_text: Is the maximum separable index among permutations avoiding a pattern of size $k$ polynomial in $k$?
context_text: A permutation $\sigma$ contains a pattern $\pi$ (of size $k$) if some $k$ entries of $\sigma$ appear in the same relative order as the entries of $\pi$, and avoids $\pi$ otherwise. Separable permutations are those obtained from the trivial permutation $1$ by repeatedly taking direct sums (placing two permutation matrices as diagonal blocks) and skew sums (antidiagonal blocks); equivalently they are the permutations avoiding $2413$ and $3142$, or those whose permutation graph is a cograph. The separable index $\mathrm{sep}(\sigma)$ is the smallest $k$ such that $\sigma$ is a product (composition) of $k$ separable permutations. The authors' main theorem is that every permutation avoiding a fixed pattern $\pi$ of size $k$ is a product of at most $2^{2^{O(k)}}$ separable permutations; conversely, products of a bounded number of separable permutations avoid some pattern, since there are only $2^{O(cn)}$ products of $c$ of them on $n$ elements. For specific patterns the bound is much lower (avoiding the decreasing pattern of length $k$ gives separable index $O(\log k)$), but from Fox's lower bounds on the growth of pattern-avoiding classes, for almost all patterns of size $k$ the maximum separable index of permutations avoiding it is at least $\Omega(k^{1/4-\varepsilon})$ for every $\varepsilon>0$. The question asks whether a polynomial upper bound holds; as an easier first step, the authors suggest bringing the upper bound down to singly exponential.
paper_title: Factoring Pattern-Free Permutations into Separable ones

title: Question 1.3
statement_text: What is the parameterised complexity of computing $\mathrm{sep}(\sigma)$, and of approximating it within a constant factor?
context_text: A permutation $\sigma$ contains a pattern $\pi$ (of size $k$) if some $k$ entries of $\sigma$ appear in the same relative order as the entries of $\pi$, and avoids $\pi$ otherwise. Separable permutations are those obtained from the trivial permutation $1$ by repeatedly taking direct sums (placing two permutation matrices as diagonal blocks) and skew sums (antidiagonal blocks); equivalently they are the permutations avoiding $2413$ and $3142$, or those whose permutation graph is a cograph. The separable index $\mathrm{sep}(\sigma)$ is the smallest $k$ such that $\sigma$ is a product (composition) of $k$ separable permutations. Given $\sigma$ and $k$, the main theorem yields an FPT approximation: there is a pattern $\pi$ (of size exponential in $k$) avoided by every product of $k$ separable permutations, while every permutation avoiding $\pi$ has separable index at most $f(k)$; running the Guillemot–Marx pattern recognition algorithm then either shows that $\sigma$ contains $\pi$, so $\mathrm{sep}(\sigma)>k$, or that $\sigma$ avoids $\pi$, so $\mathrm{sep}(\sigma)\le f(k)$. The approximation function $f$ is triple exponential in $k$. The authors ask whether this can be improved, possibly up to an exact FPT algorithm parameterised by $\mathrm{sep}(\sigma)$, and whether a constant-factor approximation is possible.
paper_title: Factoring Pattern-Free Permutations into Separable ones
